articles.title: ‘Positive momentum’: Is the US war on Iran about to end?
articles.summary: Domestic pressures are injecting new life into stalled diplomatic talks, but analysts say peace still hangs by a thread.
articles.body:
Diplomatic efforts to end the United States-Israel war on Iran have gathered pace, potentially reducing the chance of another round of intense conflict.

US President Donald Trump and Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani hailed positive closed-door talks at the White House on Monday, with Trump saying he considers the war “effectively” at an end.

But amid talk of peace, both sides have boasted that their militaries are ready and Iran has come under attack .

The US “is fully locked and loaded with the best equipment ever made”, Trump said, but added there would likely be no reason to use it as negotiations with Tehran are “going very well”.

Iran pointed to the possibility of a diplomatic solution while maintaining a deterrence posture.

On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the war would “not end either through military means or by increasing sanctions”, but only through “using the language of respect”.

The comment came a day after Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had hinted at an openness to negotiations, telling the country’s leadership to end the “no war, no peace” reality.

“We can hold talks with dignity and bring the matter to an end with dignity,” Pezeshkian said.

The crushing Republican defeat in the US midterm elections earlier this month is one of the elements injecting new life into stalled diplomatic talks between Washington and Tehran, analysts say.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance both acknowledged that the conflict – which rattled the global energy market and contributed to the rising cost of living – played a significant role in the Democratic Party taking firm control of Congress.

Negar Mortazavi, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy in Washington, DC, said the Republican losses “dramatically raised the political cost of more escalation”.

“The Democratic blue tsunami, powered by progressive and antiwar candidates, pushed the party overnight toward a stronger and more united opposition to war,” Mortazavi told Al Jazeera.

US House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , who is poised to become the next speaker of the House of Representatives in January, told reporters on Monday that the Democratic Party will “end the war in Iran one way or the other”.

Outgoing Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie moved to impeach US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, setting up a potentially explosive vote in Congress just days after the midterm elections.

Mortazavi said the result gives the Democrats a stronger mandate to challenge the unpopular war.

“If Democrats unite and use their new power aggressively, they can make it increasingly difficult for Trump to continue the war, pressuring him to end it,” he added.

‘Political and strategic costs of escalation keep growing’

Additionally, Trump’s main ally in the war, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, faces an uncertain political future after the October 27 general election .

His rival Gadi Eisenkot was tasked on Saturday with forming a new government coalition that can survive the opposition of the right-wing bloc led by Netanyahu.

Mortazavi said a third element was Qatar’s intensive mediation, including high-level engagement with both Washington and Tehran, which is creating a diplomatic pathway out of the conflict.

Oil prices fell sharply on Monday amid renewed hopes for diplomatic talks, easing inflation concerns. A diplomatic breakthrough could result in a sustained reduction in energy costs and consumer prices.

“A diplomatic breakthrough is not guaranteed, but the political and strategic costs of escalation keep growing, making another round of war less likely,” Mortazavi said. “Ultimately, Trump will have to decide whether to accept a negotiated end to the war or prolong a conflict with diminishing political support.”

Iran braces for escalation as ‘breakthrough’ appears elusive

Iranian leaders have long maintained that actions speak louder than words when it comes to Washington.

US attacks against Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz and on the island of Qeshm have been a daily occurrence. Tehran has reacted by downing US aircraft and controlling marine traffic on the key waterway.

Meanwhile, the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier strike group and the US 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit and its Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group are expected to reach the Middle East later this month.

Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei on Monday accused Washington of spreading “fake news” about potential negotiations, demanding that the US accept Tehran’s seven conditions , including the removal of the naval blockade and the unfreezing of Iranian assets.

Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said accepting this “would come at a huge cost” for the Trump administration.

“Reaching a diplomatic arrangement without securing any nuclear concessions from Iran would amount to an admission of defeat, and the Americans seem reluctant to accept that,” he told Al Jazeera. “What regional countries, particularly Qatar, have been trying hard to do is bridge this gap. There is still no sign of a breakthrough on these issues.”

To break the impasse, Azizi said Trump might “launch a major but largely symbolic attack against Iran’s nuclear facilities in order to claim victory and end the war,” even if Iranians are prepared to escalate in response.

In a phone interview with C-SPAN’s Washington Journal Primetime on Monday, Trump said, “We may have to hit Pickaxe Mountain”, which the US says hosts an Iranian nuclear site being constructed deep underground.

On Saturday, Trump called US attacks against Iran’s Qeshm island, in the Strait of Hormuz, “minor strikes” targeting Iranian air defences and launchers.

Another scenario could see the US naval blockade on Iranian ports continue, in the hope of getting more concessions from Tehran.

On his Truth Social platform, Trump claimed on Monday that Gulf countries favour maintaining the blockade of Iran’s economy rather than escalating the war, which would be “approximately five times bigger than the first hit”.

Azizi argued that while this may seem like a lower-cost option for the US and its Gulf allies, it is inherently unsustainable because Tehran has made it clear – most recently with the Supreme Leader’s statement – that it sees the blockade as a continuation of the war.

“It would only be a matter of time before the Iranians decide to escalate significantly against the US naval forces involved in the blockade. It is still unclear to what extent they have the technical capability to hit US warships, but given how rapidly Iran’s missile program has been developing, one should not rule out that possibility,” the analyst said.

“And if that happens, we may end up in the same large-scale war scenario that everyone, including the US, has been trying to avoid.”

articles.title: Ocasio-Cortez doesn’t back Schumer in Senate leadership vote
articles.summary: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) declined to back Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as he prepares to seek his caucus’s support to become m...
articles.body:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) declined to back Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as he prepares to seek his caucus's support to become majority leader beginning in January.

Asked by reporters outside the Capitol if she would back her home state's senator for the top spot in the upper chamber given calls for new leadership in the party, Ocasio-Cortez said that would be up to members of the Senate.

"I think that this is a sentiment that is seen in a lot of places," Ocasio-Cortez said. "So how the Senate navigates that, that's up to their decision."

Schumer, who will turn 76 later this month, has faced skepticism and calls to step down from some younger members of his party. Multiple incoming Senate Democrats — Sens.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.), Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Troy Jackson (D-Maine) — have said they will not back Schumer for majority leader.

Still, the leader said he had secured enough support to become Senate leader, something he needs a majority of his caucus to do. After Democrats' massive victories in the midterms, the party's now-sizable majority in the upper chamber allows him to win a vote even if some Senate Democrats do not back him.

If Schumer runs for reelection in 2028, he would be 84 at the end of his next term. Ocasio-Cortez is seen as a potential challenger to Schumer in the Democratic primary but pivoted when asked if she would take him on, saying Americans do not want to hear about another election.

"The last thing that people want to hear from me or any other politician here is about the next election," Ocasio-Cortez said. "They want to know about the investigations we're going to be starting, what is the legislation that we're going to be starting … what we're going to do with the power that they just gave us."

If she does not challenge Schumer, the progressive Democrat is also seen as a possible presidential candidate in 2028. A political action committee run by progressive activists, called "Ready for AOC," recently launched in an attempt to draw her into the race.

Ocasio-Cortez has been candid that she is considering her options — presidential campaign or primary challenge.

"I think that anything is possible at this juncture," Ocasio-Cortez told ABC News' "This Week" in August.

articles.title: Nvidia spy case exposes how foreign agents target America’s corporate elite: 'He is compromised'
articles.summary: Nvidia's CEO apologized to employees for infidelity as the board launched an independent probe into his alleged ties to a suspected Chinese spy.
articles.body: Nvidia’s reported spy scandal is shaking markets and rattling the tech world, raising urgent questions about how close foreign agents can get to America’s most powerful corporate leaders. Dr. Michael Wallace, a professor at Tulane University and retired military intelligence officer with 20 years of experience, said foreign intelligence services study targets’ personal lives and interests to find ways to build trust and gain access. And it's become increasingly clear that business leaders worldwide could potentially provide access or information about the U.S. government if placed correctly. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was on Air Force One with President Donald Trump in May as part of the delegation during a summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing. He has also visited the White House a handful of times to discuss the administration's artificial intelligence (AI) agenda and Nvidia's powerful chips and selling them to approved Chinese customers. HOW US CEOS QUIETLY TEAMED UP WITH TRUMP TO GAIN LEVERAGE OVER CHINA There are now active investigations into whether U.S. national security or company secrets were compromised by Huang’s reported extramarital affair with a businesswoman allegedly recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to target the Nvidia CEO. "The goal of human intelligence is to get somebody close to a source that can either elicit information or obtain information from a person," Wallace told Fox News Digital. That access could reveal more than technical secrets, Wallace said. Someone close to a CEO might learn about business relationships, product plans, upcoming chip releases or conversations with government officials. The allegations revive longstanding U.S. concerns about Chinese corporate espionage and efforts to gain access to American companies’ sensitive technology and business information. Those concerns carry added weight in Nvidia’s case because its advanced chips are central to the artificial intelligence industry and the U.S.-China technology competition. NVIDIA CEO JENSEN HUANG APOLOGIZES AS FIRM PROBES AFFAIR WITH ALLEGED SPY "What makes it unique is that it happened this high up to this person," Wallace said. "That’s what boggles my mind." Nvidia’s board has launched an independent investigation into reports about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed. Alice, despite sharing a last name, has no relation to the Nvidia CEO. The New York Times reported that U.S. officials suspected Alice had gathered information for Beijing. Nvidia has said Huang meets with thousands of customer executives each year and that meetings with her were not unusual. The news caused shock waves across business and government, and is leading to calls for Huang to resign. HOUSE REPUBLICANS DEMAND ANSWERS FROM NVIDIA CEO OVER REPORTED CHINESE SPY TIES Huang apologized to Nvidia employees Sunday for being unfaithful to his wife, writing, "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." He did not identify the woman or describe the relationship in his message. The board said independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, would oversee the inquiry. It said it had "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised," while adding that the investigation would examine all available information. Nvidia said Huang would remain CEO during the review and had committed to cooperating. Amy Kremer, chairwoman of advocacy group Humans First, said Huang should resign and called for federal investigations. "He is compromised," Kremer told Fox News Digital. "We have to get to the bottom of this and let’s hope that he’s the only one." Kremer also called for Nvidia to lose government contracts until Huang leaves the company. She criticized his advocacy for easing restrictions on chip sales to China, arguing the reported relationship raises national security concerns. The allegations have not established that Huang knowingly shared information or that Nvidia’s technology was compromised. Trump said Monday he spoke with Huang and believed the Nvidia CEO "will be in good shape," while expressing amazement at the allegations. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Trump also said he did not think he would raise the matter with Xi. The White House declined to elaborate on whether the Trump administration would continue engaging with Huang, referring Fox News Digital to Trump’s previous comments.

articles.title: Progressive org launches campaign urging AOC to run for president while progressives eye socialist candidate
articles.summary: Ready for AOC launched a nationwide signature drive urging Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028 as DSA allies eye a socialist nominee.
articles.body: A progressive organization urging Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., to run for president in 2028 has kicked off a campaign to collect signatures nationwide in support of the congresswoman's potential run. Ready for AOC, which describes itself as a "people-powered," "grassroots" and "unaffiliated" organization, launched the campaign Monday, urging supporters of the congresswoman to ask her to run for president. "Movements like this work when they're loud and early — long before the candidate says yes. The proof isn't money. It's names. Yours makes the case louder," the campaign's website states. WATCH: AOC LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID: 'MAYBE, MAYBE NOT' The website boasts 804 signatures as of Tuesday morning, though representatives for the project claim to be aiming for 10,000 community leaders to join their mission, according to the New York Times. The group also claims to have 500 political and union leaders across 35 states on board, the outlet reported. "The goal is to build the infrastructure of a grassroots movement in the case that she decides to run, but also to demonstrate to her that, ‘Look, there is a movement behind you ready to power you to victory should you choose to run for president,'" Ravi Sahai, a spokesman for the group, told the New York Times. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI Ocasio-Cortez herself has been coy about a potential run, but hasn't ruled it out. Asked by Fox News Digital in July if she'd consider running, she replied, "I have genuinely not really weighed seriously anything past the midterm elections." However, following a sweeping blue wave in the midterms that saw voters punch ballots for numerous members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and other far-left candidates, the DSA's ranks are emboldened by the results and vocally making the case that America is ready for a far-left president. MEET THE FAR-LEFT SOCIALISTS COMING TO CONGRESS NEXT YEAR "For so long, we have been told that democratic socialists would be a liability," Gustavo Gordillo, the co-chair of New York City's DSA, said while speaking at an Astoria, Queens watch party on election night. "We've been told for so long that if we elect democratic socialists throughout the country that we won't be able to win races in Texas, in Florida. Tonight, we actually elected a democratic socialist in Tampa in a Republican MAGA-held seat," he bragged, according to state outlet City & State New York. The DSA, which will hold a citywide convention in New York on Nov. 14, will hold a vote on whether the organization will formally push for Ocasio-Cortez to run, Gordillo revealed to a crowd at the watch party, City & State reported. FAR-LEFT SURGE: MAMDANI-BACKED CANDIDATES OUST DEM ESTABLISHMENT INCUMBENTS Despite the buzz, however, Ocasio-Cortez has downplayed speculation following the election, telling reporters that Democrats need to focus on governing over running. "The last thing that people want to hear from me or any other politician is about the next election. What they actually want to hear from us is about what we are going to do with the electoral results they just gave us on Tuesday," she told reporters Monday. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, arguably the DSA's biggest success story, recently told NBC that America is "absolutely" ready for a socialist president. "We have heard time and again over the 10 months that I've been in office here in New York City, that what we're doing here can't work elsewhere, that what people are concerned about here isn't what people are concerned about across the country," Mamdani told NBC's Kristen Welker the day after Election Day. "And what we saw last night is that the struggles of Americans in Atlanta, of Americans in Allentown, are not all that different than the struggles of Americans in Astoria." AOC OPENS UP ABOUT RACE, GENDER IN WEIGHING POSSIBLE 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID Mamdani, who was frequently joined by Ocasio-Cortez while campaigning for mayor in 2025, has not specifically mentioned any potential 2028 candidate by name, but is reportedly meeting with labor and union leaders to organize a potential progressive bloc for 2028. Ocasio-Cortez was tabbed as the frontrunner to be the Democratic nominee in a July poll from New Hampshire Granite State, however a more recent poll from Atlas Insights had her tied with Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga. Gavin Newsom and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif. Fox News Digital contacted Ocasio-Cortez, Ready for AOC and the Democratic Socialists of America for further comment.

articles.title: Analysis: Hegseth fights for his political life with appeal to Trump
articles.summary: The defence secretary may be facing impeachment, writes Gary O'Donoghue, but it is Trump who could determine his fate.
articles.body:
There was plenty of defiance and rhetorical venom from Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Tuesday, as the under-pressure US defence secretary gave his first news conference in six months.

Much of his ire was directed at the Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, who has brought articles of impeachment against him. Hegseth dismissed him as "one disgruntled and defeated congressman" who was leading a "farce and a stunt".

But this was, in many ways, a news conference with an audience of one - President Donald Trump.

Again and again, Hegseth tied his fate to that of the president.

The military operations in Iran and Venezuela that are now at the centre of impeachment proceedings, he said, were "ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself". If standing with the president put him in the firing line, he added, "I'll take that company every day of the week".

Hegseth has frequently echoed the president's rhetoric and public statements and he did it repeatedly on Tuesday. Attacks on the media, denunciations of political enemies and even reflecting the very words the president uses.

Referring to Trump's 2019 impeachment over a call with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky , Hegseth described it as a "perfect phone call" – the exact formulation the president has used when discussing the issue.

But behind the defiance and these public demonstrations of loyalty to Trump, Hegseth is now in a much weaker position - and in a fight for his political life.

Republicans have just lost both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, with polls indicating the Iran war and its impact on voters' pockets was at the heart of their unhappiness.

Vice-President JD Vance, meanwhile, has said bluntly that the war is why Republicans lost .

Asked this morning about the political consequences of the war and Vance's comments, Hegseth avoided disagreeing openly with the vice-president. But he said the war was "not necessarily popular" but necessary – perhaps the closest he has come to accepting that Americans have soured on the enterprise.

Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'

Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war

With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle

Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly

All of this leaves this president with an impossible dilemma.

If he opts to keep his defence secretary, it risks looking as though he has not heard the message from voters.

Fire him, and it risks looking like an admission that the Iran war has become a damaging domestic liability.

A scalp or a scapegoat, put it how you like, may be necessary if Trump is to move on.

Even the promotion of Stephen Miller to White House chief-of-staff provides less comfort than it might appear. He and Hegseth are close allies, and Hegseth today called him an "incredible American patriot".

But Miller reportedly clinched the job after arguing that the White House needed to wind down the Iran war – putting a clear level of distance between the Pentagon and the president.

For the time being, Hegseth has the president's backing – but as everyone knows in Washington. a full-throated endorsement from Trump can, in the blink of an eye, evaporate into nothing if a sacrifice is required.

Votes in Congress will be the focus on Tuesday as impeachment proceedings against Hegseth get under way.

But in reality, it is the president's feelings that will likely be the ultimate arbiter of Hegseth's political fate.

articles.title: Sotomayor lets loose on conservative Supreme Court with revealing wish: 'Crazy things'
articles.summary: Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor called the presidential immunity ruling in Trump v. United States one she hopes gets overturned in her lifetime.
articles.body: As Republicans reel from their bruising midterm election losses, Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor is hoping some of the court's biggest conservative rulings will eventually be overturned. Speaking at a weekend civics education event at George Washington's Mount Vernon estate, the liberal justice singled out the court's landmark 2024 presidential immunity ruling, which shields presidents from criminal prosecution for actions taken within their core constitutional powers and provides presumptive protection for other official acts. Her colleagues, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, are both in their late 70s, raising questions about their potential retirements and whether a Democratic-controlled Senate could complicate Trump's efforts to replace them with fellow conservatives. "We saw the outpouring of voters on Tuesday … I tell people all the time, there’s no excuse for not voting. There just isn’t. Apathy is not acceptable," Sotomayor said at TRUMP'S SUPREME COURT MAJORITY FACES LOOMING THREAT AFTER DEM SENATE TAKEOVER: 'STUCK' "I dissent a lot. I’m hoping that the court will take back some of the crazy things that it’s done. I’m only joking — maybe not," she said at the same event. "No, seriously. You know, I’ve spoken openly about this, there’s some opinions that I hope in my lifetime will get overturned. The immunity case is one of them." The justice spent most of the hourlong event discussing the importance of civics education, stopping at times to discuss the state of American democracy. At one point, Sotomayor remarked that it would take "some hard work" for the United States to get back on an "even keel." SUPREME COURT JUSTICE KAGAN WARNS SOME CONSERVATIVE RULINGS HAVE BEEN 'DESTRUCTIVE OF OUR DEMOCRACY' "There have been some systemic changes in my court’s jurisprudence in many areas of law," she stated. "We’ll settle down, too. Not quite sure when. But we will. And a new order will be established that people will begin to understand." Sotomayor specifically singled out the Supreme Court's 2024 landmark ruling on presidential immunity as something she would like to see revisited. DEMOCRATIC SENATOR ACCUSES BIDEN ADMINISTRATION OF 'COMPLETELY' CHICKENING OUT ON SUPREME COURT REFORM In Trump v. United States, the case in question, the court ruled that former presidents have absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for actions within their core constitutional powers and at least presumptive immunity for other official acts. The justices ruled that former presidents have no immunity from prosecution for unofficial conduct, leaving lower courts to distinguish between official acts protected by the decision and private conduct that remains subject to criminal prosecution. Sotomayor sharply criticized the ruling in her 2024 dissent, arguing that the court's conservative majority had effectively turned the president into a "king above the law." articles.title: Dead felons, dog and now a prisoner: Spanberger voting rights letters draw fresh scrutiny
articles.summary: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's voting rights restoration push sent a notice meant for a woman still incarcerated on a felony conviction.
articles.body: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's voting rights restoration effort is facing fresh scrutiny after a state letter indicating that voting rights had been restored was mailed in the name of a woman who remains incarcerated on a felony drug conviction. Spanberger and Secretary of the Commonwealth Candi Mundon-King have faced criticism over a series of apparent errors, including a letter sent to a dog in Goochland County that died five years ago, another sent to a sheriff’s office in Hampton Roads addressed to "Betty No Last Name" and others mailed to the families of deceased felons. A Virginia resident who requested anonymity contacted Del. Tom Garrett, R-Buckingham, after receiving a voting rights restoration letter addressed to "Kayla Renae Vaughn," a source told Fox News Digital. DEM AG'S ELECTION CRUSADE AGAINST TRUMP RUNS INTO EMBARRASSING DEAD-FELON BLUNDER BACK HOME Fox News Digital obtained images of the letter from the Republican minority caucus in the Virginia House of Delegates. The document appears identical to other restoration letters previously reported, except for the recipient's name. The resident has no known connection to Vaughn, according to the GOP caucus. Meanwhile, Vaughn remains in prison at the Central Virginia Correctional Unit in Chesterfield County, serving a 40-year sentence with 37 years suspended. Vaughn was charged in Pearisburg in May 2023 with "Drugs: Manufacture/Distribute; Schedule I or II; Second Offense," according to state correctional records. She was sentenced in January 2025. Fox News Digital sought comment from Vaughn and prison officials. The prison referred the inquiry to the Virginia Department of Corrections, which acknowledged receiving the request. Virginia House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, a Republican, demanded an explanation from Spanberger. TROUBLING DISCOVERY ON STATE VOTER ROLLS SPARKS ACTION DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS: ‘SHOULD HAVE BEEN FIXED’ "Restoring the rights of the dead is a failure. Restoring the rights of a dog is an embarrassment," Kilgore said, citing previous cases. "Restoring the rights of someone still incarcerated on a felony conviction would represent a new level of carelessness. The Governor owes Virginia answers, and soon," Kilgore said. Garrett did not respond to a request for comment but has previously criticized the administration's handling of voting rights restoration. The letter signed by Spanberger and Mundon-King stated that the administration had a "completed review of the particulars of [Vaughn’s] case." Garrett recently pointed to a lawsuit filed by former Virginia House Speaker Bill Howell, R-Stafford, challenging then-Gov. Terry McAuliffe's attempt to restore voting rights to felons through a "big, blanket order." The Virginia Supreme Court ruled that restoration decisions must be made individually, a precedent Garrett argues is relevant to the current controversy. "[L]ook at the letters coming out of Governor Spanberger’s office. Every one of them claims the administration ‘reviewed the particulars of your individual case," Garrett said, citing the previous letter addressed to "Biscuit Rigsby," a dog in his district. "They know the rule. They’re just betting no one notices the gap between what the letters say and what actually happened," said Garrett. Spanberger and Mundon-King did not respond to requests for comment. Spanberger has publicly described her restoration efforts as benefiting "people who had previously been convicted of a felony, had served their time, returned home, and simply wanted the dignity of being able to fully participate in our democracy," a description that does not apply to Vaughn, who remains incarcerated. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The voting rights amendment approved by Virginia voters on Nov. 3 also limits automatic restoration to people who have been "once released from incarceration." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The amendment provides for restoration without requiring individual action by the governor. It excludes people "serving a sentence of incarceration for a felony" and those who "do not understand the act of voting."

articles.title: Trump's first Iran war escalation post-midterm losses seeks to choke off Tehran’s trade
articles.summary: President Donald Trump launches Task Force Iron Gate to choke off Iran's land borders, but experts warn squeezing Tehran could trigger escalation.
articles.body: President Donald Trump isn't backing off his pressure campaign against Iran despite claims the conflict contributed to sweeping Republican losses in last week's midterm elections. In fact, Trump is doubling down by expanding U.S. efforts to choke off the trade routes Tehran increasingly relies on as it tries to rebuild its military in the midst of war. The new effort, dubbed Task Force Iron Gate, takes aim at a vulnerability that has persisted despite the U.S. naval blockade: the land and Caspian Sea routes Iran can use to bring in goods, dual-use technology and military supplies beyond the reach of American warships. That approach, one expert claims, fits into a broader administration strategy of tightening the squeeze on Tehran while stopping short of restarting full-scale military operations. Meanwhile, others caution that it could produce escalation rather than an immediate diplomatic breakthrough. IRAN VOWS ‘ASTONISHING’ STRIKES AND LIFTS MISSILE-RANGE LIMIT AS US TARGETS LAND ROUTES "We have Operation Iron Gate that just went into effect. That means nothing comes in by land," Trump said Sunday. But the roughly 20-person task force established at U.S. Central Command headquarters in Tampa is taking a quieter approach than Trump’s sweeping description might suggest. "This is not a deployable special operation task force," Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told Fox News Digital, describing Iron Gate instead as a "fusion cell" coordinating military, civilian and intelligence efforts. US ECONOMIC CHOKEHOLD ON IRAN REACHES PEAK LEVERAGE AS COLLAPSE RISKS EMERGE Nadimi said its immediate role is likely to center on gathering intelligence about activity along Iran’s borders and building cooperation in the region that could support sanctions and other efforts to disrupt the flow of goods. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who heads the department responsible for spearheading the administration's diplomatic foreign agenda, supports taking action that could decrease military escalation. "We don't need to conduct military strikes if we're achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure," Rubio told reporters on Tuesday. He rejected the suggestion that the U.S. and Iran were at a stalemate, arguing that sanctions, the naval blockade and other measures were steadily weakening Tehran. "They’re bleeding. They’re bleeding economically," Rubio said. "It is an increased pressure on Iran that continues to grow every day." The push comes a week after an election in which the war proved a political liability for Republicans. The Iran war was a crucial factor in the House vote for 34% of voters, according to the Fox News Voter Poll, while about six in 10 said the U.S. had made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran. A separate Fox News/NORC survey conducted around Election Day found 68% said avoiding a prolonged military conflict in Iran was very important. When forced to choose, 61% said ending U.S. military involvement to lower gas prices was more important than restarting military action to stop Iran from developing nuclear weapons, while 35% chose restarting military action. Yet four days after the election, CENTCOM announced Iron Gate, extending the administration’s pressure campaign to the land routes Tehran could use to blunt the effects of the naval blockade. CENTCOM said the task force would coordinate efforts to disrupt advanced weapons, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue moving across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea. "We will not allow the Iranian regime to rebuild its weapons factories or replenish its arsenal with materials smuggled across its borders," CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in announcing the task force. CENTCOM declined to provide additional details about how Iron Gate would operate beyond its announcement. The challenge is the sheer scale of the territory involved. Iran shares land borders with Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey and Turkmenistan, spanning roughly 6,000 kilometers, according to Nadimi. While it has dozens of official border crossings, goods can also be smuggled through mountainous and desert terrain. "It will be extremely difficult to know where and how things get in or out of Iran," Nadimi said. Much of Iron Gate’s effectiveness will also depend on governments outside Iran. Nadimi said the task force could build relationships with military and intelligence services in neighboring countries to identify and disrupt suspicious shipments. Turkey and Pakistan have already placed some limits on goods moving across their borders with Iran, he said, contributing to long truck lines and higher shipping costs. But even if neighboring governments cooperate, Iran and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps are likely to look for ways around the restrictions. Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the effort should not be judged by whether Washington can completely eliminate Iran’s overland trade. "That is not going to mean zeroing out this trade overnight," Taleblu told Fox News Digital. Instead, he said the goal is to increase the cost of moving goods, pressure the foreign companies and individuals facilitating Iranian trade and give Washington more leverage over Tehran. "This is literally akin to boxing in the Islamic Republic," he said. The routes have taken on added importance as Iran’s other avenues to the outside world have narrowed. Taleblu said Iran’s missile program remains dependent on foreign inputs including fuel precursors and high-strength steel. China and Russia are important to those flows, he said, but Iraq, Turkey and Pakistan also represent important regional routes. Nadimi described effectively restricting Iran’s land trade as a "mid- to long-term project" and predicted Tehran would initially "become more aggressive" as the pressure mounts. Taleblu issued a similar warning. That leaves the administration trying to increase its leverage over Iran without reigniting the full-scale fighting voters strongly signaled they wanted to avoid — while Trump has publicly described the objective in much starker terms. "Nothing comes in by land."

articles.title: US Senate advances major bill boosting energy infrastructure
articles.summary: Rare bipartisan bill requires data centres to pay for infrastructure, but environmental groups say it falls short.
articles.body:
The United States Senate has voted to move forward on a bipartisan bill that would speed up the process to build new data centres and energy infrastructure in the country.

Nearly all of the chamber’s Republicans, as well as more than a dozen Democrats, voted 73-25 on Monday to take up the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which supporters, including US President Donald Trump, have said is necessary to meet the nation’s growing demand for electricity.

“This Bill is a BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE”, Trump posted on social media Monday as he encouraged lawmakers to support it.

The legislation would overhaul the permitting process for major energy projects – both clean energy and fossil fuel-run – across the US, reduce deadlines for environmental reviews and impose restrictions on when projects can be challenged in the country’s courts. It would also force owners of energy-hungry data centres to pay for the infrastructure that is needed to power them.

Growing anger in the US over those facilities’ use in powering artificial intelligence (AI) , which has resulted in rising electricity bills for customers across the country, helped fuel last week’s takeover of the US Congress by Democrats.

“The people sent us a very clear message on Tuesday that they expect us to lower the costs in their daily lives,” Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich, the ranking member on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, said on Monday. “We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs. We can do that today.”

Authors of the bill claim it will provide $19bn in savings on residential electricity bills through 2040. The number of solar and wind projects connecting to the US electric grid would be doubled, with data centres paying $55bn over the next 10 years to cover their power usage.

But despite the bill’s claims of increasing clean energy projects, environmental organisations are opposed to the legislation. They argue it would also lock in development of fossil fuels, weaken environmental laws and make it harder for US residents to challenge projects in their communities.

Earlier this year, a coalition of national groups – including the Climate Justice Alliance, Indigenous Environmental Network and Western Environmental Law Center – issued a joint statement opposing the bill.

“We cannot allow the lies to continue, as the facts are clear: If this backroom permitting reform deal is pushed through, it will enable a no-guardrails buildout of dangerous projects that will harm our health and environment, drive up energy costs, and violate our rights,” they said in September.

“This will be especially harmful for communities of color and lower income neighborhoods already overburdened by pollution and climate impacts.”

While the legislation received rare overwhelming support from both major political parties, the Democrats’ midterm win could complicate its final passage.

Some in the party argue that the legislation should be shelved until new Democratic majorities in the US House and Senate are sworn in early next year.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is on track to become the body’s new speaker in January, criticised the bill last week, warning it “falls short” in several areas.

“We must once again support the clean energy economy and combat the climate crisis with the fierce urgency of now,” a Jeffries spokesperson said in a statement released to the Associated Press.

Jeffries’s office added: “Leader Jeffries will not rubber-stamp legislation that emerges from the Senate without more constructive involvement with our Caucus as we fight to make life more affordable for the American people.”

articles.title: Trump closing in on new press secretary as administration officials push for pick who could break the mold
articles.summary: President Donald Trump wants a man as his next press secretary, and insiders say Ben Ferguson's name keeps coming up, a source close to the president says.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: President Donald Trump is closing in on a new press secretary, and administration insiders are advocating for a person who will break the mold "His name has been brought up to the president by many people," a source close to the president told Fox News Digital Tuesday, referring to conservative commentator Ben Ferguson. "[Trump's] instincts are to pick a man," the source said. "Which many people have told him that's a good idea." LEAVITT OPENS UP ON HELPING TRUMP FIND NEW PRESS SECRETARY AFTER ZACHARIA DEBACLE: 'WAS NOT FOR HER' The source said Trump intends to choose someone to fill the vacant position soon and that he values the role of press secretary in the administration. A second person familiar with the matter confirmed Trump is planning to pick a man as his next press secretary and said Ferguson is a frontrunner. The last seven press secretaries, spanning Trump's second term, former President Joe Biden's single term and Trump's first term have all been women. Sean Spicer was the last man to serve in the role. He was Trump's first press secretary from January 2017 to June of that same year. He was replaced by Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who is now governor of Arkansas. Ferguson is a conservative commentator who hosts the nationally syndicated radio show, "The Ben Ferguson Show." He's also a political commentator on CNN. But Trump is still weighing his options. "POTUS is not sold on the idea," the source said of Ferguson. "I think it's safe to say [Ferguson is] pursuing the job, and the president is aware." Scott Jennings, the conservative CNN contributor who frequently appears on "Newsnight with Abby Phillip" and worked in former President George W. Bush's administration, is also in the running for the job. "The president keeps going back and forth on Scott Jennings," the source said. "I don't think it will happen." A few other names have been floated but not emerged as clear picks for the job. This includes White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Breitbart chief Matthew Boyle and Ari Fleischer, who was White House press secretary during President George W. Bush's first term. Many woman have also made the short list, but the two sources who spoke with Fox News Digital insist the next person to hold the job will likely be a man. ALINA HABBA SHUTS DOWN SPECULATION SHE COULD REPLACE KAROLINE LEAVITT AS WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY Ferguson has support from within the Trump administration, Fox News Digital has learned. "Ben is one of loudest supporters of President Trump in the 21st century," a senior White House official told Fox News Digital. "While many supporters don’t have the courage to take to the fake news, Ben consistently walks into the lion’s den and faces the media bias head on." The official said Ferguson runs circles around some people who are currently paid to defend Trump. JEN PSAKI MOCKS TRUMP’S NEW PRESS SECRETARY, QUESTIONS IF SHE’S A 'POTENTIALLY FAKE LAWYER' "His resumé and experience are exactly what the administration will need when they face a Congress hell-bent on dismantling our efforts to Make America Great Again," the official continued. Another Trump administration official echoed that sentiment, claiming, "Ben has always been a skilled and talented commentator." "He and Scott are screamed at by the radical left everyday as they defend the president to a hostile audience," the official said, adding that the hostility the pair face on cable news is not unlike what they would face standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room. "The president needs a tireless, talented communicator at the podium who’ll relay his success for the nation and how he’ll be a bulwark against Democrats’ attempts to dismantle our Republic," the official said. The White House has been without a press secretary since Oct. 13, when Katie Zacharia left the job at Trump's urging after only a week. Zacharia's brief tenure was marked by controversy over her claims to be an attorney and a disastrous press conference that lasted only 14 minutes and was widely condemned as a train wreck. Leavitt resigned from the post in August after returning from maternity leave, citing a desire to spend more time with her growing family.

articles.title: House GOP report on Jeffrey Epstein rips Justice Department, urges further investigation
articles.summary: The House Oversight Committee’s review of the investigation into Jeffrey Epstein blasted the Justice Department’s handling of the case from the outset and in the decades since, and called for federal investigators to take a closer look at the late sex offender and his associates.
articles.body: The House Oversight Committee’s review of the investigation into Jeffrey Epstein blasted the Justice Department’s handling of the case from the outset and in the decades since, and called for federal investigators to take a closer look at the late sex offender and his associates. “One thing is abundantly clear in the Epstein matter: the federal government failed over the course of decades and multiple administrations to ensure justice and protect Epstein survivors,” the committee’s Republicans said in a report released Tuesday. “DOJ must make renewed efforts to provide this needed justice and accountability to Epstein survivors.” “Too many survivors and other witnesses informed this Committee that they were never approached or properly questioned by federal authorities,” the 137-page report continued. “The DOJ should interview or, in some cases, reinterview key individuals who were part of the inner circle of Epstein and Maxwell,” a reference to Epstein co-conspirator Ghislaine Maxwell. In a statement, Committee Chair James Comer, R-Ky., said, “Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims.” “The evidence we uncovered makes clear that the Department of Justice must interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records,” Comer said. In a statement, a Justice Department spokesperson said, “With all due respect, the Chairman’s recommendations have already been addressed. The Attorney General has repeatedly said that the Epstein case is not closed and there is no statute of limitations on human trafficking.” “The Department will continue following all additional investigative leads in matters relating to Jeffrey Epstein. Any victims with evidence and information are encouraged to reach out to the FBI,” the statement said. The wealthy and politically connected Epstein died by suicide in his jail cell in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges. He’d previously been investigated on charges he sexually abused dozens of women and girls over a decade earlier, but cut a deal with federal prosecutors in 2008 that allowed him to plead guilty to state charges involving a single underage victim. The deal resulted in Epstein serving 13 months in a Palm Beach County jail, where he was allowed to leave almost daily through a work-release program and have his own private security detail. He could have faced up to life behind bars had he been convicted in a federal complaint that was shelved as a result of the deal. The Justice Department and FBI said in a joint memo last year that Epstein had preyed on more than 1,000 victims, but the only other person to be charged in the case was Maxwell, who was convicted of sex trafficking and conspiracy charges in 2021 and is serving a 20-year prison term. That joint memo said there was no evidence showing that other people should be charged in the investigation, and despite earlier vows to the contrary from top administration officials, no further information about Epstein’s case would be released. The political backlash to that memo led to the passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA), a law the mandated that documents related to the case be made public. Millions of pages of documents have been released, but some are still being withheld or were released with what critics have said are too many redactions. “Despite extraordinary efforts undertaken by DOJ staff to expedite the release of EFTA records, questions remain as to whether the DOJ has released all relevant documents,” the report released Tuesday said. The Republican report chided the department for releasing names of some victims in documents that it said should have been redacted, while redacting the names of Epstein allies who it said should have been identified. “These failures underscore the importance of meaningfully engaging with and working alongside victims to ensure their privacy is protected and their concerns are considered before sensitive records are released,” the report said. “Survivors of the crimes of Epstein and Maxwell also continue to ask the DOJ for their own means of accessing their personal files and documents. As of this report, DOJ has not permitted that to occur.” The House report said one way Epstein was able to operate was by getting his victims to sign nondisclosure agreements. The report called for Congress to “pass legislation protecting the ability of individuals with knowledge of sexual abuse and survivors to speak freely about these crimes, regardless of nondisclosure agreements.” The top Democrat on the committee, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, said in a statement that the Republican investigation was “incomplete,” and that Democrats will continue the probe when they take the majority in January. Comer held “zero public hearings” on Epstein, and DOJ “continues to illegally withhold over 2.5 million pages of documents,” Garcia said. “We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation,” Garcia said. “We intend to hold real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump. Our work is just getting started.” Democrats on the committee released their own report last month that called for an independent special counsel to investigate Epstein’s ties to President Donald Trump. The two had a social relationship that ended before Epstein was first hit with criminal charges. The Democratic report alleged the Justice Department worked to cover up Trump’s connections to Epstein, and said an independent special counsel is necessary because Attorney General Todd Blanche was compromised because he was Trump’s personal attorney before joining the administration. Blanche has defended the Justice Department against the criticisms that it took too long to release the files and mishandled redactions, saying, “You’re talking about working through 6 million pieces of paper.” The White House said the allegations in the Democratic report were untrue and politically motivated. Trump has denied any knowledge of or involvement in Epstein’s criminal activity and said he had a falling out with Epstein because he thought he was a “creep.” The Republican report ripped Democrats for focusing on Trump in their own findings, saying they were “obsessed” with the president and had engaged in an “unfounded witch hunt.”

articles.title: Peltola widens narrow Alaska Senate lead over Sullivan as counting continues
articles.summary: Mary Peltola's lead over Dan Sullivan grew to 2,517 votes after Monday's ballot drop, but tens of thousands of absentee ballots remain uncounted.
articles.body: Alaska's still too-close-to-call Senate race is expected to deliver another batch of ballot results Tuesday night after Monday's latest ballot drop expanded Democratic nominee Mary Peltola's lead over incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan to 2,517 first-choice votes. Still current as of Tuesday midday ET, Peltola stands at 48.6% (106,321 votes) to Sullivan’s 47.5% (103,804) in the ranked-choice voting system that will kick in if neither candidate gets across the 50% threshold. The controversial race, punctuated by the "Decoy Dan" scheme exposed by The New York Times, has Republican Gerald Heikes at 2.2% (4,865) and independent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 1.7% (3,651 votes). Roughly 75–76% of the expected vote is in, with tens of thousands of early, absentee and questioned ballots still to be counted. ALASKA SENATE FIGHT HEATS UP AS SULLIVAN MOVES TO BLOCK PELTOLA LAWSUIT OVER REJECTED ABSENTEE BALLOT RECORDS "After every vote is counted, it is clear that Mary Peltola will be elected Alaska’s next United States Senator," Peltola campaign manager Cheryl Bruce wrote in a statement Tuesday morning after that previous tranche of votes. "Mary won today’s votes by a margin of 68-30, reflecting major support in key areas from Anchorage and Chevak. This overwhelming margin further strengthens Mary’s path to victory, and Mary is looking forward to continuing her relentless fight to lower costs and put Alaska first in the United States Senate after all votes are counted." Monday's drop added nearly 5,000 ballots and marked a shift from the razor-thin, 637-vote Peltola edge that had held for days after Election Day. The incumbent Sullivan and President Donald Trump have both suggested if Peltola does not get to 50% of the vote and ranked-choice voting (RCV) goes to rounds two or three that the Republican would absorb secondary voting strength in the system. DOJ FACES ‘HEAVY LIFT’ IN ALASKA ELECTION APPEAL AS SEPARATE CRIMINAL PROBE CONTINUES Under Alaska’s system, if no candidate reaches a majority of first-choice votes, the lowest finisher is eliminated and ballots transfer according to voters’ rankings until one candidate surpasses 50%. Right now, that would be the other Dan Sullivan, which might help Peltola break 50%. The Official RCV tabulation is scheduled for Nov. 18 after the overseas absentee deadline. The slow pace matches the timeline Gov. Mike Dunleavy described in an interview Sunday. He called the state’s process "very confusing" and "a slow system," pointing to significant ballot dumps expected Friday, Nov. 13, and Wednesday, Nov. 18. Dunleavy has also continued an investigation into the "Decoy Dan" candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., which some Republicans allege was intended to siphon votes from the incumbent; the governor has said the Division of Elections and the Department of Justice are reviewing related questions. TRUMP ADMIN PUTS ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' CONSPIRATORS ON NOTICE IN ALASKA ELECTION SPOILER PROBE "We're still in the process of bringing in votes and counting votes," Dunleavy said Sunday. "And we are in the midst of investigations as to determine if there was any wrongdoing, especially anything that might resemble perjury or, you know, a misrepresentation of individual's intent on how they wanted their candidacy to be placed on the ballot." Other statewide races remain fluid on the same ballot count: MURKOWSKI SNUBS TRUMP-BACKED ALASKA CANDIDATE, ENDORSES DEMOCRAT FOR GOVERNOR Certification is set for Nov. 25. articles.title: Shanghai-based tycoon Neville Roy Singham's 'Squad,' Bernie Sanders donations resurface
articles.summary: FEC records show Neville Roy Singham and CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans have donated a combined $47,000 to Bernie Sanders, Pramila Jayapal and more.
articles.body: A Shanghai-based tycoon known for pushing Chinese Communist Party talking points, whose activist network is flooding Capitol Hill this week, has directly funded some of the most powerful progressives in Congress, including members of "The Squad." Federal Election Commission records show that Neville Roy Singham and his wife, CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans, have given more than a combined $47,000 to Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Reps. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Chuy García, D-Ill. Omar's campaign took $4,200 from the couple from 2019 to 2023, according to FEC records. Singham gave her campaign $2,700 in March 2019, just weeks after she took office, and Evans gave $1,500 in two contributions in November and December 2023. None of it has been refunded. HOUSE PANEL TO PROBE FOREIGN ‘TROJAN HORSES’ AS SINGHAM SCRUTINY WIDENS Sanders' campaigns have taken in at least $6,800 from the couple, according to FEC records, most of it for his presidential bids. Singham gave $2,700 to Sanders' 2016 presidential campaign. Evans gave the 2016 campaign $2,800, of which it refunded $200, and at least $252 to his 2020 campaign in 2019. She also gave $1,250 to his Senate campaign committee, Friends of Bernie Sanders, in 2011. García's campaign took in $1,000 from Singham in August 2018, according to FEC records. He was running for his first term in Congress at the time, after winning the Democratic primary for Illinois' 4th Congressional District, Singham's home city of Chicago. The campaign has not refunded the contribution. Jayapal has received more from the couple than any other member of Congress, a net $35,700 from 2016 to 2022, according to FEC records. Singham gave her campaign $17,800 and none of it was refunded. Evans gave $22,900, and the campaign refunded $5,000 of it in three payments between 2020 and 2023, leaving $17,900. Most of the couple's money came in 2019 and 2021, including back-to-back maximum contributions from Singham in both years. Under Federal Election Commission rules, a campaign has 10 days to decide whether to deposit a check or return it. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's, D-NY, campaign returned a $500 contribution from Evans through ActBlue on the day it arrived, Aug. 4, 2018, during her first run for Congress. Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of Sanders, Jayapal, García and Ocasio-Cortez and Omar's office for comment but did not receive responses. DHS, WAR DEPT JOIN PROBE INTO SINGHAM NETWORK ALLEGEDLY SOWING DISCORD IN US After his wedding to Evans in 2017 and the sale of ThoughtWorks, the technology company he founded, Singham directed $285 million to nonprofits and media organizations, according to a Fox News Digital investigation. The People’s Forum received $22.4 million from Singham, while CodePink received $1.33 million. BreakThrough BT Media Inc., which operates BreakThrough News, received $1.098 million, according to tax filings. Singham and his wife, who are both American citizens, now live in Shanghai, China. Organizations within the Singham network regularly participate in staged anti-ICE, anti-capitalist, anti-data centers and anti-Israel protests – many of which garner national and social media coverage. FROM AUSTIN TO NEW YORK, PRO-CHINA NETWORK FUELS WEEK OF ANTI-US PROTESTS AS XI MEETS TRUMP Last month, Evans and CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin embarked on a China propaganda tour across the communist country. The trip, according to an event promotion link for sign-up on the CodePink website, was 12 days and 11 nights in Shanghai, Chongqing, Zunyi, Loushanguan, Maotai Village and Guiyang with the cost of attendance between $3,000 and $4,000 depending on the total number of participants. The CodePink website said attendees will be "greeted by local Shanghai comrades," and a tour with Benjamin and Code Pink co-founder Jodie Evans is included. "Explore China’s revolutionary history, while marveling at high-tech infrastructure and modern socialist development," the event description reads. "Highlights include Red Memorials, Historical Re-Enactments and Museums, Socialist Infrastructure, and Rural Revitalization." Singham’s wife’s California-based nonprofit does not shy away from their mission to rebrand China as an ally – displaying the tagline "China is not our enemy" on their website while actively promoting the "revolutionary history" of the communist country. HOUSE PANEL SUBPOENAS 3 LEFT-WING GROUPS IN PROBE OF $39M TIED TO MARXIST TYCOON NEVILLE SINGHAM A slew of federal and congressional investigations have been opened into the Singham network, including a grand jury probe led by the Department of Justice and the Southern District of New York – though Singham has yet to be charged with any crime. During a House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia committee hearing in September, Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation, cited research saying Singham shares premises with Maku Cultural Communication, a Chinese communications firm that promotes a favorable image of China, and was photographed attending a Chinese Communist Party strategic communications workshop in 2023. JIM BANKS, GOP LAWMAKERS RALLY BEHIND DOJ PROBE INTO ALLEGED CCP-LINKED FUNDING NETWORK In a video that Fox News Digital unearthed, Singham stood at the Golden Tulip Hotel in Shanghai during a November 2025 conference and expressed support for "a new world order that is based on multilateralism that President Xi and the CPC [Communist Party of China] and China have proposed." Earlier this year, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent traveled to New York City for a meeting with Goldman Sachs Chairman and CEO David Solomon, and sources told Fox News Digital that Bessent gave a blunt ultimatum to Solomon. Bessent told Solomon that Goldman Sachs could face scrutiny for alleged conspiracy in the funneling of the Singham money and urged Solomon to cooperate with federal investigators. A person familiar with the meeting told Fox News Digital that the discussion wasn't contentious and that Solomon readily agreed to pledge his cooperation with the Justice Department investigation. A spokesperson for the bank said "all distributions from Mr. Singham’s donor-advised fund were made to legal nonprofits, as determined by the IRS. There have been no distributions from the account since August 2023, and it was closed in early 2024." articles.title: US House Republicans choose Jim Jordan as their next party leader
articles.summary: By David Morgan WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - House Republicans chose Jim Jordan on Tuesday to lead them in opposition to a Democratic-controlled Congress,...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - House Republicans chose Jim Jordan on Tuesday to lead them in opposition to a Democratic-controlled Congress, according to a person familiar with the matter, putting a combative Donald ‌Trump ally at the forefront of the party's fight to defend the US president's agenda during his ‌final two years in office.

A secret ballot held behind closed doors elevated the Ohio Republican and House Judiciary Committee chairman to the minority leadership post ​a week after Democrats swept to victory in last Tuesday's midterm elections, winning sizable majorities in both the House and Senate.

House Speaker Mike Johnson opted not to stand for the leadership position.

Across the Capitol, Senate Republicans met behind closed doors to decide whether to push forward with internal elections that were expected to retain US Senator John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, as the ‌party leader or opt for a delay that ⁠could allow a challenger to emerge.

The House and Senate leadership elections will help determine what role Republicans intend to play as the minority party in Congress during the final two years ⁠of Trump's presidency.

Democrats will need Republican support to move major initiatives in the 100-member Senate, where the filibuster rule requires 60 votes for most legislation. Their majorities in both chambers also fall well short of the two-thirds votes needed to override presidential vetoes.

After the ​midterm ​elections, Thune vowed that Republicans would work with Trump to block "Democrat ​extremism" and work against any attempt by Democrats ‌to unwind Republican achievements including border security and judicial appointments.

Jordan, 62, was first elected in 2006 to represent a deeply conservative rural district in northern Ohio and was a founder of the House Freedom Caucus, a group that former Republican Speaker John Boehner labeled "legislative terrorists."

Before entering politics, Jordan honed his pugilistic style during a career as a high school and university champion wrestler, and later as a wrestling coach at Ohio State University.

That past threatened his political career in 2018 when former ‌students accused him of turning a blind eye to rampant sexual ​abuse of college wrestlers by the wrestling team's doctor, when Jordan was ​an assistant coach.

Jordan denied all allegations, and a university ​investigation found no hard evidence that he knew of the abuse. But former wrestlers said ‌the doctor's abuse was well-known and the report itself ​found that students had complained ​about the doctor's voyeurism in front of coaching staff.

Jordan has often referred to his wrestling background in terms of his reputation as a fighter in Congress.

He is known for his aggressive style of questioning in committee hearings.

"I ​look at it like a wrestling match," ‌Jordan told the New York Times in an April 2023 interview, explaining how he prepares for hearings. "I'm ​going to try to get as ready as I can. You can't just wing it."

(Reporting by David ​Morgan; Editing by Michael Learmonth, Alistair Bell and Howard Goller)

articles.title: US voters want Democrats focused on ending Iran war, lowering costs: Poll
articles.summary: Poll shows majority of Americans want Congress to prioritise addressing rising cost of living and economic challenges.
articles.body:
A new poll shows that the majority of Americans want the Democrats in Congress this January to deliver an end to the war in Iran , reverse US President Donald Trump’s trade policies , and bring down the high cost of living.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found that 71 percent of Americans supported Congress passing legislation to end the war with Iran, including 93 percent of Democrats and 51 percent of Republicans. About 62 percent backed repealing Trump’s import tariffs, while nine in 10 respondents said Congress should focus on the cost of living during its first 100 days.

The war with Iran and Trump’s tariffs have both contributed to economic pressures , linking voters’ concerns about living costs to the administration’s foreign and trade policies.

Americans also expect some degree of cooperation between the White House and the incoming Congress. Large majorities of respondents from both parties said it was important for Trump to work with Democrats, and for Democratic leaders to try to work with the president.

Political retaliation against the Trump administration is a lower priority. Forty-two percent said it would be bad for the country if the new Congress tried to impeach Trump, compared with 33 percent who thought it would be good.

Democrats will have between 54 and 56 Senate seats next year, depending on results from uncalled races in Mississippi and Alaska. But delivering on voter priorities could still be difficult. Most bills need 60 votes to overcome a Senate filibuster, and Trump can veto legislation that passes both chambers.

Repealing tariffs or reversing other administration policies would therefore require either sufficient Republican support or a willingness to confront the president politically.

Seth Masket, a political science professor at the University of Denver, said voters are motivated by opposition to the Trump administration on several fronts, including the economy, the war, corruption and immigration enforcement.

“They want to see Democrats working to fix these things. And also to some extent, to hold the Trump administration accountable,” Masket told Al Jazeera.

The pressure to deliver on those priorities is unfolding alongside a growing dispute over who should lead the Democratic Party.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll did not measure public support for individual congressional leaders. It did, however, find that the Democratic Party itself remains unpopular, with 45 percent of respondents viewing it favourably and 51 percent unfavourably.

Hakeem Jeffries is widely expected to become speaker of the House, despite calls for an alternative. No challenger has publicly emerged, but a Change.org petition urging Democrats to reject his leadership has attracted more than one million signatures. House Democrats are due to hold leadership elections on November 18 and 19.

The Senate contest is less settled. Chuck Schumer , who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, faces calls to step aside. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has said Schumer should not receive a “blank check” and is considering a possible challenge. Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has backed Van Hollen.

The backlash reflects broader dissatisfaction with the party’s direction. Jeffries and Schumer have been criticised over their positions on Israel and Gaza, their relationships with corporate donors and pro-Israel lobbying groups such as the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), and what voters see as a failure to confront the Trump administration forcefully.

The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which counts several elected officials among its members, has not backed Jeffries or Schumer for their respective leadership posts. In a statement to Al Jazeera, the DSA said Democrats must reject “half-measures” and deliver on popular policies.

“We the people must be a counterweight both to the internal politics of Congress and the corporate donors who want to keep business as usual,” DSA spokesperson Priscilla Yeverino wrote to Al Jazeera.

Political commentator Bea Neilson said some progressives see the two leaders as representing an older Democratic establishment that is out of step with the party’s base.

“They want an avatar of a fighter,” Neilson told Al Jazeera.

But Neilson argues that the role of the House speaker is not simply to dictate the party’s legislative agenda. Rather, they respond to the positions of lawmakers across the caucus, working with policy committees and other groups to identify legislation that can secure enough votes to pass.

Individual members or blocs of lawmakers can withhold their support, making the job an exercise in negotiating competing interests as much as setting political direction.

Masket agreed that the effectiveness of congressional leaders is often measured less by their public speaking than by their ability to manage their caucuses and get legislation through Congress.

“People wanting their speaker or a Senate majority leader to be a more inspiring leader, I think they’re just asking for the wrong person,” Masket said. “That’s the wrong title for that role.”

That role, he suggested, may fall more naturally to the next generation of presidential contenders , who are expected to begin emerging early next year.

The leadership elections will take place before the new Congress begins in January. The larger question for Democrats is whether their leaders can turn a sweeping electoral mandate into tangible change.

articles.title: BJP’s youth conventions to win over Gen Z and blunt opposition’s growing outreach
articles.summary: BJP to hold 296 UP campus youth conventions titled “Loktantra vs Arajakta” to counter SIR “vote chori” claims and pitch Yogi govt’s jobs, law and order record.
articles.body: Lucknow: The incidents of paper leaks, recruitment controversies and alleged irregularities in SIR of electoral rolls have spurred BJP to take its political battle to college campuses to win over Gen-Z and blunt the opposition’s growing influence among the youth ahead of UP elections.The party plans to organise 296 youth conventions in prominent educational institutions in all six organisational regions of the state. Spearheaded by Bharatiya Janata Yuva Morcha (BJYM), the proposed campaign, titled ‘Loktantra vs Arajakta’ (Democracy versus Anarchy), will seek to counter the opposition’s allegations over SIR and the ‘vote chori’ narrative while projecting Yogi govt’s record on employment, law and order and governance against that of the previous Samajwadi Party govt.BJP also plans to invoke the Emergency (1975) and the 1984 anti-Sikh riots to portray Congress and its allies questionable record on democratic values.The campaign reflects BJP’s recognition that the battle for UP polls may not be confined to traditional caste and community equations, but could increasingly hinge on how parties engage with a generation of voters whose concerns over jobs, recruitment, reservation and educational opportunities are shaping the political discourse.UP BJYM president Rohit Mishra told TOI that the conventions would sensitise young voters about the “undemocratic” functioning of previous govts and the changes brought about by Yogu govt.“Young people need to be reminded of the lathicharge during the previous SP govt when they took to the streets demanding their share of govt jobs. They also need to understand the difference between the governance models of the two govts,” Mishra said.He added that the campaign would be launched soon after the constitution of BJYM’s state executive committee over the next few days.The initiative is being viewed as an extension of BJP’s increasingly combative political strategy following Union home minister Amit Shah’s recent offensive against Congress and other opposition parties. Having sought to counter the Congress-led ‘vote chori’ campaign by defending electoral reforms and the SIR exercise, BJP is now looking to take that argument directly to young voters rather than leave the political narrative to be shaped by its opponents.“Youth supporters of the BJP are most active in different areas including spreading awareness about SIR,” said UP BJP spokesperson Priyank Pandey.Party sources said the campus interactions would seek to establish that the opposition was deliberately creating confusion over electoral reforms and attempting to undermine the credibility of democratic institutions. BJP also hopes to use the conventions to build a counter-narrative around the Emergency, electoral integrity and the functioning of constitutional institutions.The regional distribution of the 294 conventions indicates the scale of the proposed exercise. The western region and Braj region will organise 57 conventions each, Kanpur 51 conventions, Kashi 48, Awadh 45 and Gorakhpur 38 conventions.BJP’s campus outreach is not merely about countering the Opposition’s allegations over SIR. It also comes at a time when the party is confronting a more complicated challenge: addressing the growing expectations and anxieties of young people over employment, competitive examinations, reservation and higher education.Sources said controversies surrounding UGC regulations and reservation-related issues have emerged as sensitive subjects among sections of the students. The party wants its youth leaders to engage directly with students, gauge their concerns and address grievances before these develop into wider political discontent.Political observers feel that BJP’s decision to focus on educational institutions is significant given the opposition’s attempts to make unemployment, alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations and reservation central to its political campaign.
