articles.title: Top Dem cries ‘weaponization’ as comments warning young people not to join Trump admin land her in hot water
articles.summary: Dem Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., cries "weaponization" after Trump ordered the Justice Department to investigate her remarks warning young Republicans about joining his administration.
articles.body: Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., is accusing President Donald Trump of escalating a coordinated "weaponization" campaign against her after he ordered the Justice Department to examine remarks she made warning young Republicans they could face "a ton of problems" if they joined his administration. In a Truth Social post over the weekend, President Trump accused Democrats of political weaponization and singled out Slotkin for "go[ing] after all young people that believe in Republican values" in her October remarks. "By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!" Trump wrote. In a video response posted Monday, Slotkin defended her remarks, saying she was referring to people who might be asked to violate the law or misuse taxpayer dollars and citing her First Amendment rights. "A couple weeks ago, I talked about how anyone who is violating the law or misusing taxpayer dollars should be held accountable, and if there's young people who are thinking of joining people who are doing that, they should think twice," Slotkin said. "If you're not violating the law — no problem." DEMS PIVOT FROM 'AFFORDABILITY' PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS Slotkin said Trump began targeting her after her October remarks, first by "name-checking" her from the Oval Office before he "really ramped up his coordinated play" following Democrats’ midterm election gains. She also pointed to Attorney General Todd Blanche's Sunday television appearances discussing possible investigations. Slotkin said her attorney sent the Justice Department a letter Monday asking, "What are you going to do?" The Justice Department has not confirmed whether it has opened an investigation into Slotkin. During an interview Sunday on CNN’s "State of the Union," Blanche declined to identify a specific crime when asked whether Democrats’ rhetoric could constitute one, saying, "It depends on what’s said. So, yes, it could be." A DOJ spokesperson separately told NBC News that Slotkin’s comments should be evaluated under the facts and law but did not confirm an investigation. Fox News Digital reached out to the DOJ for comment but did not hear back in time for publication. OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE AT CENTER OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WEAPONIZATION FUND CASE HIT WITH MISCONDUCT CLAIM Slotkin's original remarks also prompted a congressional ethics complaint. Michael Bicksel, a University of Chicago student who first publicized her comments, filed the complaint with the Senate Select Committee on Ethics on Oct. 22. Bicksel argued that Slotkin had proposed using congressional investigations and potential prosecutions to deter young people from joining a Republican administration, asking the committee to determine whether her comments amounted to "improper conduct which may reflect upon the Senate." Fox News Digital reached out to Slotkin for comment but did not hear back in time for publication. "It's a coordinated, manufactured response," Slotkin previously said about the backlash to her remarks concerning young Trump supporters. "They want to intimidate you to be quiet." Slotkin made the remarks Oct. 13 during a University of Chicago discussion about how Democrats could exercise congressional power if they regained control of Congress. Fox News Digital previously reported that Slotkin advocated pursuing "signature cases" against people who enabled Trump rather than focusing exclusively on the president. She also argued that the prospect of legal trouble could deter young Republicans from joining his administration. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The latest dispute follows an earlier Justice Department investigation involving Slotkin and five other Democratic lawmakers who posted a video reminding military personnel and intelligence officials that they were not required to follow unlawful orders. A federal grand jury declined to indict the lawmakers. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER In a letter to Blanche made public Monday, Slotkin's attorney, Preet Bharara, argued that her remarks were protected by the First Amendment and the Constitution's speech or debate clause. Bharara demanded that Blanche publicly confirm the Justice Department would not investigate the senator. "Just like last time, Senator Slotkin will not be deterred," Bharara wrote. "She will continue to call out corruption by this administration and to exercise her First Amendment rights to speak out against the President’s many abuses of power."

articles.title: Jamie Raskin calls concerns over spending too much time investigating Trump a media 'narrative'
articles.summary: Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., dismissed concerns within the party about Democrats in Congress focusing too much on Trump investigations as a media "narrative."
articles.body: Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., called concerns that the incoming Democratic Congress will focus too much time investigating the Trump administration a media "narrative" on Monday. During an interview on "CNN News Central," host Brianna Keilar noted that Adam Hamilton, a Democrat recently elected to the U.S. Senate, said that he doesn't "want to spend the next two years in trials" against the Trump administration after Democrats regain control of the House and the Senate. "This is something that we're hearing from a lot of those Democrats who did come in," Keilar said. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH Raskin attempted to interrupt Keilar and later dismissed the concern as a "narrative," despite Keilar's reference to comments from an incoming senator. "That's a narrative the media is trying to drive, but–" Raskin said. "Well, I'm just quoting him, right? So this is what he said. So is he, are other Democrats going to be disappointed by the amount of time spent on investigations?" Keilar said. Raskin answered, "No, because we have lots of committees. We have got a brilliant new class of Democratic representatives and senators coming in, and we're going to be able to do it all. We're going to be able to get Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act, health insurance back to the American people. Millions of people have been thrown off of their health plans because of the actions of the Trump administration and their wretched, hideous bill. We're going to be able to restore people's benefits to food in the SNAP program." CRENSHAW, RASKIN SHOUT EACH OTHER DOWN IN HEATED POST-MIDTERM DEBATE He added, "We're going to be able to get rid of these ruinous 50% tariffs on Canada and on the rest of the world and begin to bring prices down. If they're all serious in running away from Donald Trump and not wanting to have anything to do with the Iran war anymore, beginning with JD Vance, then they can bring us a plan for how we can extricate from the mess that they have given us in Iran. We can work together on all those things. That will bring gas prices and diesel prices down. We can all work together. Corruption and affordability are really the same issue here with the Trump administration, as usually they have been." Fox News Digital reached out to Raskin's office and Hamilton's campaign for comment. Although Raskin initially suggested these concerns were part of a media "narrative," several prominent progressive figures have gone on the record discouraging congressional Democrats from spending the next two years targeting President Donald Trump. PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP One of them included Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who made his comments as recently as Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press." "Do we want to hold the Trump administration accountable for their corruption, for their illegal, unconstitutional actions? Absolutely," Sanders said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He stressed that Congress must not focus solely on investigating Trump when issues like high child poverty rates, senior poverty, and economic and privacy threats posed by AI require urgent action.

articles.title: Those who denied Ram’s existence are now maligning Ayodhya: Yogi
articles.summary: Yogi Adityanath says Ayodhya development has rattled SP, Congress; inaugurates 52 projects worth Rs 82.41 crore in Gorakhpur during Diwali event.
articles.body: Gorakhpur: Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Sunday targeted the Samajwadi Party (SP) and Congress, accusing them of spreading propaganda against Ayodhya after failing to stop the city’s transformation through heritage and development. “Those who used to say that Ram never existed are now engaged in maligning Ayodhya,” he said, asserting that the political future of both parties would be at stake if the development journey continued at the same pace.Yogi made the remarks while celebrating Diwali with the Van Tangiya community at Jungle Tinkonia No. 3 village in Gorakhpur. He shared the festival’s joy with the community for the 10th consecutive year as chief minister, after overseeing the Deepotsav celebrations in Ayodhya on Saturday.He also inaugurated and laid the foundation for 52 development projects worth Rs 82.41 crore related to rural development, eco-tourism and the Global Nagar Bazaar initiative.Greeting people on Diwali, Yogi referred to the construction of the Ram temple and the rapid development of Ayodhya and Uttar Pradesh, saying that anything was possible with determination. He recalled that before 2017, people were allegedly prevented from chanting “Jai Shri Ram” in Ayodhya and that opposition parties had opposed the Ram temple movement.He said roads, electricity, airports, railway lines and public facilities had expanded since the BJP government came to power in Uttar Pradesh in 2017.The chief minister said the Van Tangiya community had been left to struggle in forests for more than a century under British rule and successive Congress and SP governments. He said 56 Van Tangiya villages in Uttar Pradesh had remained deprived of basic amenities, including voter registration, roads, electricity, drinking water, ration cards, schools, healthcare, pensions and pucca houses, even after Independence.Yogi said development initiatives undertaken after 2017 had transformed the villages. articles.title: Could Protect College Sports Act be running out of time? Randy Levine sounds the alarm
articles.summary: The Protect College Sports Act faces an uncertain future in the House. Randy Levine is turning up the heat on Congress.
articles.body:
Randy Levine has ratcheted up the rhetoric and pressure on the U.S. House of Representatives over the Protect College Sports Act .

On Tuesday, Nov. 10, Levine sent a letter to the House, obtained by USA TODAY Sports, that told representatives, in part, "If the PCSA passes, there will be nothing to prevent collective bargaining in the future if the law changes in the future."

And his missive has nothing to do with Tuesday night's second edition of the 2026 College Football Playoff rankings , which have sparked their own controversy over the past week.

As president of Major League Baseball's New York Yankees and President Trump 's Roundtable on Fixing College Sports, Levine used the 800-word letter to paint in stark terms what he believes will happen if the PCSA passes, or if it fails.

"It is not debatable that if the PCSA passes, student-athletes will receive major benefits that they do not have today," Levine wrote.

"Members of Congress, the ball is in your court. It is the ninth inning, fourth quarter, third period. The nation is watching. Will it be petty politics, anger and division, or will it be a bipartisan consensus coming together for the public good?

"History will remember if you choose wrong. Pass the PCSA."

The 200-plus-page bill sailed through the Senate with 77 votes and has been publicly touted by Trump. Bill co-sponsor Ted Cruz (R-Texas) repeatedly has called for the measure to be whisked through the House and placed before Trump to sign live on ESPN's "College GameDay."

Levine touted funding for HBCUs, women's sports and Olympic sports as key elements of the legislation while saying "special interest groups" are again working to thwart the bill.

"Almost every university and college in the country, both large and small — about 400 of them — want the PCSA passed," Levine wrote. "Why? Because without it, these schools believe their financial health will seriously continue to decline. They will have to raise tuition and fees, cut scholarships, and eliminate women's and Olympic sports programs just to stay afloat. Yes, college will become less affordable for every student. And with fewer scholarships available, fewer students will have the opportunity to earn one.

"So, too, it is no secret that HBCUs are reeling in financial distress. The PCSA provides a billion dollars or more lifeline to them. Yet despite the fact that the PCSA received 77 votes in the U.S. Senate — a remarkable and overwhelming bipartisan show of support — as the legislation moves to the House, the same special interests that tried to kill it in the Senate are at work again."

A lobbyist who has worked directly with a Power conference and individual P-4 schools told USA TODAY Sports this week of the PCSA: "It's dead." The individual spoke on condition of anonymity to provide candid thoughts about the bill's prospects.

Elsewhere, a proponent of the measure on Capitol Hill who has worked directly on the act shared the following with USA TODAY Sports:

"There is no realistic path to secure the same broad, bipartisan support for a new bill in 2027 and beyond. Passing the Senate-approved bipartisan bill through the House and sending it to the President's desk during the lame-duck Congress gives House Republicans an opportunity to close out the 119 th Congress with a significant win for President Trump, HBCUs, women's sports, and student athletes. An attempt to amend it would be a surefire defeat for the colleges and fans counting on the PCSA's enactment."

As the lobbyist noted, "the primary issues facing Congress" during the post-election period include "Government funding, which halts on Dec. 11, 2026; defense authorization, healthcare and policy extenders, farm bill and agriculture."

Additionally, the lobbyist said nominations and judicial confirmations are expected to be wedged onto the Senate calendar before newly elected members of Congress take office in January 2027.

articles.title: Senate GOP rebellion fizzles as Thune keeps power despite historic midterm massacre
articles.summary: John Thune secured another term as Senate GOP leader despite Ron Johnson and Rick Scott pushing to delay elections after midterm losses.
articles.body: There was neither an exodus nor a mass housecleaning in the Senate GOP leadership, despite frustration and rumblings of discontent among some lawmakers reeling from last week’s devastating midterm losses. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., secured another term as the top Republican behind the closed doors of the Old Senate Chamber, where lawmakers charted their course for their few remaining weeks in power and beyond. Thune, along with the bulk of his leadership team, which now includes Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, were swiftly elected after a group of Republicans failed to delay the leadership elections. It wasn't without a fight though, with conversations behind closed doors dragging on for over seven hours. GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., led the charge to delay, and didn't stick around after his attempts to do so failed on a 31 to 15 vote in the Old Senate Chamber to proceed with the scheduled election. Johnson and others wanted to have a deep conversation about what had happened during the midterm elections, and a roadmap on what Republican leadership candidates could accomplish with the little time they had left in power. SENATE GOP REBELS MOVE TO DELAY LEADERSHIP VOTE, DEMAND RECKONING AFTER MIDTERM DISASTER But there was no opposition to any of the lawmakers running for leadership. "This has never been anything against John Thune," Johnson said. "I think he has been very unfairly attacked, you know, by our base, and I don't agree with that. What I didn't agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position." On Monday, Thune was adamant that he’d still run but was unsure of the outcome. "That's the hope," Thune said when asked if he had the Senate GOP’s support. "You never know right until they vote." Before the vote, Johnson and a handful of others believed there should be a shakeup in leadership, but didn’t offer an alternative to Thune. "After the stunning defeat, you just can't continue on business as usual," Johnson said. "I mean, that kind of defeat demands change." When asked if he’d be interested in running, Johnson said, "That’s part of the problem. Would you want it?" "I think there's a number of people with talent," Johnson said. "Again, I'm not — at a minimum, we need to see out of our leadership team what's the strategy moving forward, and you can't come off of a defeat like that and just ram through elections and oh yeah, ‘let's just elect that leadership team by acclamation.’" Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., had previously run for leader twice and most recently against Thune. But the lawmaker, who joined Johnson’s crusade for change, declined to throw his hat into the arena again. "I think we have to acknowledge the voters are not happy," Scott said. "We have to start listening to voters." CONGRESS RETURNS TO BRUTAL LAME-DUCK STRETCH WITH SHUTDOWN DEADLINE, LEADERSHIP RACES: 'CLOSET IS FULL OF S—' Scott wanted ironclad promises on the GOP’s to-do list, including ramming through judicial nominees, government funding "without a massive omnibus," a stock trade ban, permitting reform, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, taking another crack at the SAVE America Act and balancing the budget — possibly through budget reconciliation. Johnson and Scott were joined by Sens. Ted Budd, R-N.C., Mike Lee, R-Utah, John Kennedy, R-La., Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Dave McCormick, R-Pa., in a push to delay the elections that was not met, and the would-be coup faded as the secret ballots were cast. Still, there were others outside that cohort who weren’t happy with last week and believed that there should be deeper soul-searching on what Republicans did over the last two years that led to a historic night for Senate Democrats. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., contended that much of what the GOP listed as accomplishments over their time in power is what worked against them. "And, you know, you have the kind of record that this Congress has had, I think we better have a pretty tough family conversation about what it is we're doing," Hawley said. "When you cut Medicaid, but you fund data centers, when you cut rural hospital funding, but you fund Planned Parenthood, when you let the cost of healthcare for working people go through the roof, but you can't do anything for them on other issues of affordability, from fertilizer to gas," he continued. "Yeah you know what? The public doesn’t like that very much."

articles.title: Voice of America head was illegally fired by Kari Lake, court says, backing reinstatement
articles.summary: A federal appeals court panel on Tuesday said former Voice of America (VOA) head Kari Lake illegally fired former director Michael Abramowitz, backing his reinstatement in the role. The three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit found that Lake fired Abramowitz without independent approval amid the Trump administration’s attempts to…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court panel on Tuesday said former Voice of America (VOA) head Kari Lake illegally fired former director Michael Abramowitz, backing his reinstatement in the role.

The three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit found that Lake fired Abramowitz without independent approval amid the Trump administration’s attempts to dismantle the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM), the VOA’s parent agency.

“We conclude by considering remedy. Defendants assert that the district court lacked authority to enjoin them from removing Abramowitz without the Broadcasting Board’s approval,” the panel wrote . “That argument, too, is foreclosed by our precedent … Defendants contest the district court’s power to enjoin Abramowitz’s removal, but they point to nothing to counter his contention that no other form of relief would redress his injury.”

Abramowitz said in a statement obtained by Politico that he was “gratified” by the ruling and said he looked forward to returning “to the important work Voice of America does worldwide on behalf of the American people.”

The appeals court unanimously upheld the ruling made by Senior Judge Royce C. Lamberth of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia last year determining that the USAGM did not have the authority to fire Abramowitz and that the Reagan appointed judge could reinstate Abramowitz.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

Lambert ordered in March that VOA rehire its employees more than a year after President Trump significantly downsized USAGM, accusing the administration of a “flagrant and nearly year-long” refusal to uphold congressional mandates by dwindling its staff and resources.

In April 2025, Lamberth indefinitely blocked the administration’s attempts to dismantle VOA.

Abramowitz and a handful of VOA reporters, unions and the international free press advocacy nonprofit Reporters Without Borders sued the Trump administration over its effort to disband VOA.

Lake, who Lamberth ruled was leading the agency unlawfully, was an outspoken critic of the broadcaster and defended the administration’s attempts to overhaul its operations. She said she “strongly” disagreed with Lamberth’s ruling that she illegally led the agency.

“The American people gave President Trump a mandate to cut bloated bureaucracy, eliminate waste, and restore accountability to government,” Lake said in a statement previously obtained by The Washington Post . “An activist judge is trying to stand in the way of those efforts at USAGM.”

Trump signed an executive order in March 2025 to gut USAGM, which also oversaw several other networks around the world, like Radio Free Europe and Radio Free Asia.

articles.body:
Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said he would do all he could to help Sen.-elect James Talarico during the transition after the incumbent and his successor met on Capitol Hill for the first time post-election.

“I told him I’ll be happy to help him all I can during the transition,” Cornyn told TMZ . “It’s normal. It used to be normal.”

Talarico won Cornyn’s Senate seat last week after the incumbent lost renomination in a May primary runoff. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton beat Cornyn with Trump’s endorsement but lost to Talarico by a margin of 12 points. Previously, Texas had not elected a Democrat for Senate since 1988.

Cornyn stopped to talk to reporters in the Capitol multiple times Tuesday and was frequently asked about Talarico and the midterms.

“He seems like a nice guy, and I wish him well,” Cornyn said, according to Punchbowl News. “He’s gonna have an interesting time navigating a red state as a Democrat.”

“If he does a good job representing 32 million Texans, I’ll be cheering him on,” he added. “If he wants to try to advance the radical agenda of some members of his own party, I’ll be doing everything I can to fight him.”

Cornyn argued that Texas is still a red state, despite the fact that Democrats captured every statewide race and flipped the state house in the midterms.

Sen. Ted Cruz, one of the only remaining statewide elected Republicans in Texas, disagreed with that notion in a lengthy social media post after the election, professing that “Texas is blue.”

Cruz announced new headquarters Tuesday for the Saving Texas nonprofit run by his allies. Located in Austin, the headquarters will focus on recruiting and electing GOP candidates in the Lone Star State.

Asked by TMZ if he thinks Talarico and Cruz will be able to work together, Cornyn said, “I don’t think they have any choice.”

“They’re going to have to work together, represent 32 million people,” Cornyn said. “I’m sure they’ll work it out, and because I’m sure they both have the best interest of the people of Texas at heart.”

In his post-election statement, Cruz said he had spoken to Talarico to congratulate him on his “very impressive victory.”

“It was a pleasant conversation, and I told him that I looked forward to working with him to try to benefit Texas,” Cruz said.

articles.body:
Former President Biden has revealed the contents of what he described as a “very generous” letter his predecessor President Trump left him in the Oval Office in 2021, offering a glimpse of goodwill between the political foes after a bitter presidential election.

In the letter, published in full in Biden’s upcoming memoir, “Promise Me, America,” Trump praised Biden’s love for the country and expressed confidence in his ability to lead, according to an excerpt obtained by The New York Times .

“You now have the opportunity to choose your place in history, and I know you will be true to yourself and the American people,” Trump wrote in the letter, dated Jan. 20, 2021.

“Many presidents have come and gone who simply governed as Republicans or Democrats,” he continued. “Largely, they did not change history, they were just swept along in its relentless tide. This will not happen to you because I know how much you love the American people.”

The letter was left in an envelope addressed “To ‘46,’” referring to Biden’s place in the presidential succession. Biden told reporters shortly after taking office that Trump had left him a “very generous letter,” but declined to disclose its contents.

The White House confirmed the letter’s authenticity to NewsNation, saying in a statement that Biden did not heed to the president’s words.

“Joe Biden should have heeded the President’s wise words, but instead he tried to destroy this country and weaponize the justice system against his political enemies. Biden is a disgrace, and America is better off with him no longer as president,” White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said in a statement.

The letter stands in sharp contrast to Trump’s public treatment of Biden, whom he repeatedly attacked during the 2020 presidential campaign before refusing to concede his election loss. Trump also broke with tradition by declining to attend Biden’s inauguration, which took place two weeks after his supporters stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

In Biden’s book, set for release on Nov. 17, the former president acknowledged the contradiction, writing that it was “as if there were two Donald Trumps.”

Trump had “deeply destabilized our democracy” and refused to meet with him before leaving office, Biden wrote.

articles.body:
CMS blocks $112M in Medicaid funding to Minnesota

The Trump administration is cutting off more than $112 million in federal funding to Minnesota over “unallowable claims,” the most recent escalation in the White House’s fight over Medicaid fraud in the state.

The administration sought to block hundreds of millions of dollars in Medicaid funding to blue states this year, including Minnesota and California over allegations of fraud. It has made Minnesota a focal point in President Trump’s fraud crackdown.

In a letter to Minnesota Department of Human Services temporary commissioner John Connolly, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services cited dozens of instances where Minnesota allegedly failed to provide necessary documentation or provider documents where certain dates didn’t align.

But Connolly is questioning how the administration decided which claims to challenge, and whether officials confused documentation mistakes with fraud .

“We have more questions than answers right now, including CMS’s extrapolation methodology and how they selected the 330 claims for review in a quarter with more than 6 million high-risk claims,” Connolly said in a message to leaders in his department on Tuesday.

“CMS’s findings indicate the basis for the disallowance is administrative paperwork deficiencies, including issues with signatures, signoffs, dates and addresses in billing, as well as other supporting documentation,” added Connolly. “We are actively reviewing information in the attached letter we received late Friday and plan to request more information from CMS before determining next steps.”

Minnesota has 60 days to appeal the disallowance by CMS.

Connolly said CMS in the past year has not responded to numerous requests for “transparency, partnership and a path to resolution.” He noted CMS has still not made any determinations regarding two earlier funding freezes totaling $350 million .

Medicaid is jointly funded by the state and the federal government. If CMS never pays Minnesota, the state may have to ask providers to give the money back

articles.body:
Key Democrats shrug as Trump bashes wind

Key Democratic negotiators on Tuesday shrugged off President Trump’s Monday remarks that he would not approve wind projects despite his support for a bipartisan bill that seeks to boost all forms of energy.

The bill in question, which aims to ease the path forward for various forms of energy including renewables and fossil fuels, cleared a major procedural hurdle on Monday with significant bipartisan support.

Minutes before the Senate started to vote on the matter, Trump said he would not approve more wind turbines.

“The bill hasn’t been fully negotiated,” he told reporters. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

On Tuesday, however, Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) expressed confidence that wind projects would move forward under the administration.

“As long as the agencies continue to come through with the representations and promises that they have made — and we will see more of that in the next few days — then on we go, and we chalk that up to him being 80,” Whitehouse told reporters.

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) is projected to win reelection to her seat in Florida’s 27th Congressional District despite breaking with President Trump on his immigration agenda during the campaign, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

She is set to clinch a narrow win over Democrat Eliott Rodriguez, in the south Florida district, notching about 50.2 percent to her opponent’s 49.8 percent, with more than 95 percent of the vote tallied Tuesday evening.

Salazar made headlines in September when she posted a video criticizing the president for the execution of his immigration agenda. She said Trump had gone “too far” and that Hispanic Trump voters felt “betrayed” by the president. Salazar said she doesn’t support amnesty for immigrants without legal status but a “dignified life in this promised land.”

In September, Trump said he still supported Salazar even after the video bashing him. Trump said Salazar doesn’t have a “very strong feeling” in regard to border security but affirmed his support for the Florida Republican anyway.

DDHQ forecast Salazar as the likely winner of the race even after polls sponsored by Democrats showed a tight race in early September. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) traveled to the district to campaign for Salazar’s opponent.

Issues highlighted on her campaign website include small business and the economy, healthcare, public safety and fighting socialism. Salazar was raised in Miami by parents who fled Cuba following Fidel Castro’s rise to power.

articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) reacted Tuesday to the election loss of his former son-in-law, Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), saying he wished the House lawmaker “nothing but, actually, rehabilitation” — an apparent reference to his high-profile domestic abuse allegations.

“Look, as you know, that had nothing to do with politics for me,” Moreno told TMZ DC’s Charlie Cotton in a clip posted to the social platform X , responding to a question about Miller’s failed reelection bid in Ohio’s 7th Congressional District.

“It’s an ongoing family issue that I hope gets resolved,” Moreno added. “Honestly … he’s the father of my granddaughter. I wish him nothing but, actually, rehabilitation and to actually be a good dad.”

Moreno’s daughter — Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno — accused the House lawmaker earlier this year of physically abusing her and her child. In August, when the allegations gained widespread attention, Sen. Moreno called on Miller to resign, saying at the time his former son-in-law needed “serious psychological help.”

“If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives,” Moreno wrote on social media this past summer.

“I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does,” he added.

Miller faced increased political pressure throughout his re-election campaign after his ex-wife alleged in court filings he had tossed hot water on her, held a gun to her head and broke their daughter’s collarbone during their relationship. The Ohio representative denied the claims and later sued Emily Moreno for defamation.

Last week, Democrats notched an upset victory in Ohio, with Democrat Brain Poindexter unseating Miller — who had served two terms. The upset came as a surprise to the GOP, as President Trump won the district by double-digits in 2024.

articles.body:
Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) gave President Trump a failing grade for his performance in South Carolina’s midterm elections after a Trump-backed Senate candidate defeated Norman in the Republican primary but lost to a Democrat in the general election.

“In South Carolina, he gets an F,” Norman told MeidasTouch on Tuesday when asked to grade Trump’s performance in last week’s midterms. “But overall for the country, he’s done well.”

Norman argued Trump deserved a failing grade because of his decision to endorse Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), over him in the primary.

“He shouldn’t have endorsed and tried to force a candidate on South Carolina. They don’t agree with that,” Norman said.

Graham, who filled her brother’s seat following his death in July, lost her bid for a full term to Democrat Annie Andrews, delivering a stunning upset in a state where Republicans have held both Senate seats for decades.

Although Norman pledged to support Graham in the general election following his defeat in the primary, he refused to campaign alongside her and said his family would not vote for her. Trump traveled to South Carolina in the closing days of the campaign to rally support for Graham, but she ultimately fell short.

“This race shouldn’t even be close, and it wouldn’t be if I were in the race,” Norman said in a radio interview days before the election.

His son, Warren Norman, also publicly rejected Graham’s candidacy, writing in an op-ed published by FITSNews that he was leaning toward voting for Andrews , a pediatrician.

Darline Graham was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) to temporarily fill the vacancy left by her brother, who died unexpectedly. It was the first time a sibling was sworn in to replace a senator who died in office.

articles.body:
Cruz says Hegseth will resign, be fired or get impeached

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) predicted on his podcast earlier this week that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will either resign, be fired or be impeached in the latter half of President Trump’s second term.

“And one of two things is going to happen: either Hegseth is going to step down, either he will resign voluntarily or Trump will fire him . Or, if that does not happen, I think it is extremely likely, if not certain, that the House will impeach him ,” Cruz said on a Monday episode of his podcast, “The Verdict.” “Because, on the face of it, the votes are there. Now, it only takes a majority to impeach.”

Cruz’s comments came a day before House Republicans shelved Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) eight articles of impeachment against the Pentagon chief.

The House voted 211-204 to refer the resolution, which Massie reintroduced on Monday, to committee — a move that essentially ends the push to impeach Hegseth in the 119th Congress.

Trump celebrated the vote outcome Tuesday evening.

“Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!) and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” the president wrote in a post on Truth Social. “The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!”

Cruz said Monday he would not be surprised if Democrats try to impeach Hegseth once they take the majorities in both chambers of Congress come January.

“And I expect, if Schumer has the option of conducting a trial, I would anticipate that he would conduct an extended trial — that he would spend real time, weeks, if not months, using the trial to prosecute, number one, their opposition to the Iran War. ”

The Pentagon took a victory lap following the House vote Tuesday evening, calling the outcome a “total victory” and deriding Massie’s salvo as a “political exercise devoid of merit, evidence, or seriousness.”

“It collapses under the weight of Secretary Hegseth’s record of restoring the warrior ethos, delivering results and putting the mission first. The American people see through it, ” Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement .

“We will not indulge the political theater driven by a disgruntled soon-to-be former congressman and others who have chosen grandstanding over governing,” Parnell said. “ We look forward to ending this sham impeachment in the committee room, where facts will continue to prevail and this distraction can be put to rest.”

articles.body:
Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon (D), who lost to GOP incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody in last week’s midterm elections, referred to the contest during an interview posted Tuesday as a “missed opportunity” for Sunshine State Democrats.

“If want to continue to profess that we care about Black people and Hispanic communities, then we need to invest in them,” Nixon said on “The Don Lemon Show.” “Black women, especially Black people, are seen as the backbone of the party, and so they need to not only invest … in our labor so to speak, they need to really invest in our leadership.”

“It was just a really missed opportunity, and we need to have some tough conversation,” she added.

In the interview, Nixon also discussed funds her campaign received from Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and other members of the Democratic Party, with some donations coming in “the day before the election” — seeming to suggest the donations may have come too little, too late.

The Hill has reached out to Schumer’s office, Nixon’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for a comment.

Florida is one of the few states where Republicans maintained their strong hold as Democrats secured sweeping victories across the country — claiming both congressional chambers and flipping GOP-held seats in battleground states like Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Kansas, among others.

Nixon lost the Senate race to her opponent by around 200,000 votes and a little less than three points, according to Decision Desk HQ , The Hill’s election results partner. The state’s gubernatorial race also swung in the Republicans’ favor, with Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) defeating Democrat David Jolly by a little over one point.

While Democrats lost statewide races in Florida, they did not lose hope for 2028. Florida Democratic Party chair Nikki Fried said she believes the left may be closer to breakthrough in future elections.

“Yes , we could win. … Imagine if we put a little more into Florida,” Fried said in an interview with The Hill, recounting her recent conversations with the party’s operatives.

articles.body:
Rep. Ken Calvert (R-Calif.) is projected to win the race for California’s 40th Congressional District against fellow California Republican Rep. Young Kim in a race determined by the Golden State’s passage of Proposition 50 last year, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ .

With 69 percent reporting, Calvert leads his fellow Republican by about 7 points. Per DDHQ, he currently has 53.5 percent of the vote to Kim’s 46.5 percent.

The new district merged Calvert’s 41st District and Kim’s 40th District. It stretches across part of Orange County and the Inland Empire in San Bernardino County, encompassing the cities Mission Viejo, Corona, Lake Elsinore and Rancho Santa Margarita.

The race was predetermined to cost one of the two California Republicans their House seat, as both candidates represented large parts of the new boundaries from their original districts. Calvert held on to a larger portion of the new district compared to Kim.

Calvert first won his House seat in 1992, becoming California’s longest-serving Republican member in its congressional delegation. The lifelong Corona resident has served on the House Appropriations Committee as chair of the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee. Calvert is also the chairman of the California Republican House Delegation.

He campaigned on his conservative bonafides, pointing at Kim’s 2021 vote alongside Democrats against a Trump-era rule to roll back regulations on methane emissions, the Los Angeles Times reported. While at a rally in Murrieta with California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton (R) and state Assembly member Carl DeMaio (R), he contrasted himself as a consistent conservative.

“People know exactly where I’m at,” he told Spectrum News last month. “I haven’t changed a bit in the 30 years, and so I’ll continue to give people the kind of common sense governance that they deserve.”

Calvert won endorsements from several large conservative and Republican organizations in the state, along with other Golden State Republican candidates like Hilton and former gubernatorial candidate and Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco.

articles.body:
The Kennedy family has jumped into a legal battle against President Trump’s proposed arch.

In a Monday court filing in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, members of the Kennedy family requested that the court bar the Trump administration “from taking any steps to approve, authorize, or construct the Arch absent congressional authorization, designation by Congress of a sponsor, and compliance with all statutory requirements.”

“President Donald J. Trump is attempting to unlawfully erect a massive arch that will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family’s honor at Arlington National Cemetery, as well as to the memorials of hundreds of thousands of fallen American heroes,” the filing reads.

Last Thursday, a federal judge ordered a pause on the construction of Trump’s triumphal arch for two weeks.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan’s temporary restraining order followed shortly after the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted in favor of the administration’s plans to erect the arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The motion passed with an 8-4 vote following over 100 public remarks, the majority against the arch, in a meeting that lasted nine hours.

The president’s planned arch would be similar to arches in other cities, like Paris’s Arc de Triomphe.

Washington, D.C. and Virginia sued the National Parks Service and Interior Department late last month to stop Trump’s arch. The District and the Old Dominion referred to the arch as “flagrantly unlawful” due to the president not seeking congressional approval for the project’s construction.

“In their rush to break ground on the Arch, Defendants have made only half-hearted gestures at complying with these requirements,” the Virginia and D.C. lawsuit reads.

The Hill has reached out to the White House and Interior Department for comment.
